title: Mammoth Cave's Tuberculosis Hospital
summary: The forgotten experiment that put tuberculosis patients in the world's longest cave - where constant 54-degree air and total darkness were supposed to cure them, and where most of them died instead.

content.intro: In 1842, a Kentucky physician named Dr. John Croghan believed he'd found the cure for tuberculosis: Mammoth Cave. The cave's constant temperature, high humidity, and pure air seemed ideal for treating 'consumption,' the disease that killed more Americans than any other. Croghan, who owned the cave, built stone huts inside the passages and moved in 15 tuberculosis patients. Within five months, two were dead and the rest were worse than when they arrived. The experiment was abandoned. The stone huts remain inside the cave today, haunting reminders of desperate medicine and good intentions gone wrong. The patients were essentially imprisoned underground - no sunlight, no fresh air, no hope. What Croghan didn't understand was that the cave's stable conditions couldn't fight bacteria, and the darkness and isolation only hastened death. The huts stand in the darkness, 180 years later, as monuments to the terrifying history of tuberculosis treatment.

sections.title: The Disease
sections.body: Tuberculosis was the leading cause of death in 19th-century America. Called 'consumption' because it seemed to consume the body from within, TB killed slowly - years of coughing, weight loss, fever, and eventual death. There was no cure, no effective treatment, no understanding of the bacteria that caused it. Doctors tried everything: fresh air, sea voyages, bloodletting, mercury, move to the mountains, move to the desert. Sanatoriums emerged - institutions where patients rested, ate well, and hoped. The germ theory of disease was decades away. In this context of desperation, Dr. Croghan's cave experiment seemed reasonable. If mountain air helped, wouldn't the purest air on Earth - underground, filtered through miles of limestone - help more?

sections.title: The Experiment
sections.body: John Croghan purchased Mammoth Cave in 1839, intending to develop it as a tourist attraction. When he noticed the cave's constant 54-degree temperature and high humidity, he theorized that such conditions might cure TB. In 1842, he built two small stone huts inside the cave and moved in 15 patients, mostly enslaved people and poor whites who had no other options. The patients lived underground for months, attended by cave guides and Croghan himself. They breathed cave air, drank cave water, and saw no sunlight. Within weeks, most were worse. The damp, dark conditions accelerated their decline. Two died inside the cave. The survivors were removed, worse than before.

sections.title: The Huts
sections.body: The stone huts still stand in Mammoth Cave's main passage, preserved by the National Park Service as historical artifacts. They're simple structures - dry-laid stone walls, wooden roofs long rotted away - barely large enough for a bed and a chair. Soot stains from oil lamps blacken the ceiling. Initials carved by patients remain visible on the walls. Park tours pass by the huts and guides tell the story of the failed experiment. The huts are among the most photographed features in the cave, not for their architecture but for their haunting history. Visitors often ask how anyone could have thought this was a good idea. The answer is desperation.

sections.title: The Cave
sections.body: Mammoth Cave is the longest known cave system in the world, with over 400 miles of surveyed passages and more being discovered regularly. The cave formed in limestone over millions of years, carved by underground rivers. Native Americans explored it thousands of years ago; their torch marks remain. White settlers mined saltpeter for gunpowder during the War of 1812. Croghan's tuberculosis experiment was one chapter in a long history of human use. The National Park Service acquired the cave in 1941. Today it hosts over 500,000 visitors annually, who come for the geology, the history, and the sheer scale of the underground world.

sections.title: Visiting Mammoth Cave
sections.body: Mammoth Cave National Park is located in south-central Kentucky, about 90 miles south of Louisville. The park offers numerous cave tours ranging from easy walks to strenuous climbing expeditions. The Historic Tour, which passes the tuberculosis huts, is the most popular. Reservations are strongly recommended; tours frequently sell out. The park also offers surface trails, camping, and canoeing on the Green River. The cave maintains a constant 54°F, so bring a jacket regardless of the weather above. Louisville International Airport is the nearest major airport. The park is accessible via I-65. Allow a full day for cave tours and surface exploration.

content.flightContext: Located at 37.19°N, 86.10°W in south-central Kentucky. From altitude, Mammoth Cave National Park is a large forested area amid Kentucky farmland - the Green River winds through the park. The visitor center and cave entrances are in the central section. The cave system extends underground for hundreds of miles, invisible from above. Louisville is 90 miles north. Nashville is 80 miles south. The terrain is classic Kentucky karst - sinkholes, disappearing streams, rolling wooded hills. Louisville International Airport is the nearest major commercial service.
